description: We’re the Thais Russomano Team from Florianópolis, Brazil. We combine electrical engineering, embedded systems, software, and data analysis to build T.H.A.I.S., a prototype that uses NASA data to help crews respond to health risks far from Earth. If you enjoy turning research into tools people can use, join us. We’d especially welcome skills in space physiology, wearable sensors, or interface design.
summary:
During long-duration space missions, crews may need to respond to health concerns before guidance arrives from Earth. We developed T.H.A.I.S. (Tech & Health Astronaut Intelligent System), a software prototype that helps crews answer two questions: how urgent is a change, and who needs to know?

T.H.A.I.S. combines public NASA records from the Inspiration4 mission, spacecraft radiation measurements, and solar particle events with clearly labeled simulated vital signs. Its rules distinguish the urgency of a finding from who can see its details. A crew-wide hazard generates a shared notice, while medical personnel can review the measurements and sources behind an alert. This approach gives each person information they can act on while keeping individual health details private. It could also support teams working far from medical care on Earth.
details:
T.H.A.I.S. (Tech & Health Astronaut Intelligent System) is a crew health monitoring prototype for long-duration space missions, where communication delays can make immediate medical guidance from Earth unavailable. It addresses two questions separately: How urgent is a finding, and who needs to see it? Urgency determines how the interface highlights a finding. The crew member’s role determines which details appear and what action the software suggests.

The prototype combines de-identified Inspiration4 laboratory records from NASA’s Open Science Data Repository (OSD-569, OSD-575, and OSD-656), spacecraft radiation measurements from NASA RadLab, and solar energetic particle events from NASA’s DONKI database. A Python simulator supplies additional signals, including heart rate and oxygen saturation. The interface labels the source of each input so users can distinguish historical measurements from simulated readings.

To identify changes that deserve review, the software compares an astronaut’s latest laboratory measurement with their own preflight baseline. It expresses the difference in units of that person’s preflight standard deviation, giving the medical team a way to judge how unusual a reading is for that individual. For trends over time, the system uses ordinary least squares and Theil–Sen regression and displays uncertainty alongside its projections. Medical personnel can inspect the underlying measurements when deciding how to respond.

The guided radiation demo shows how the audience changes the message. The crew sees a short instruction to follow radiation contingency procedures. The flight surgeon can review a DosTel1 reading from the spacecraft and a separate solar particle event recorded about 73 hours later. The interface preserves both timestamps and identifies the DosTel1 value as a vehicle measurement. This gives the crew a clear instruction while giving the medical team the evidence needed to interpret it. NASA’s OCHMO-TB-044 Medical Operations brief informed this design.

Expert feedback

  • Maisa Hortal, a general practitioner specializing in psychiatry, recommended identifying the specific types of white blood cells monitored and adding other health indicators. We implemented both suggestions in the prototype.
  • Lucas Fonseca, a mechatronics engineer and entrepreneur in Brazil’s space sector, suggested a future lunar base as another setting where crews could use T.H.A.I.S. to coordinate care far from Earth.
  • Rebeca Gonçalves, an astrobiologist and space farmer, recommended role-based access to sensitive health information and a ticket system for requesting help from the Crew Medical Officer. The prototype incorporates role-based views, and the project design includes the help-request workflow.
  • Rosa Maria Pereira Miranda, an analog astronaut at Wogel, highlighted the potential value of monitoring crew health over longer missions, when tracking changes over time could help teams better manage risks to crew members.

We built the prototype with Python, FastAPI, React, and PostgreSQL. The public web demo lets visitors explore the workflow, while the architecture supports local deployment through Docker Compose. Our next step is to test it in an analog mission and measure whether crew members recognize who needs to act, choose the intended next step, and interpret the alert correctly. Future development includes integration with physical sensors and synchronization over intermittent links. The same approach could also support field teams working far from medical care on Earth.
